Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Opinion Spain The right’s exploitation of the Ceuta migrant ‘crisis’ almost guarantees that it will happen again Ruben Andersson The EU’s panic and the lack of solidarity emboldens smugglers and the far right – and makes Spain even more vulnerable Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.33 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.54 EDT Share For the European hard right and the White House, it seemed almost too good to be true: left-liberal Spain punished with a migration crisis of its own making. The histrionics came right on cue. As thousands of mainly Moroccan citizens streamed into the tiny Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the tip of north Africa, Spain’s far-right party Vox decried a migrant “invasion”, blaming Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s regularisation and leftist politics. The Trump administration did the same. A senior Israeli diplomat goaded Madrid over its “colonial” territories while Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area. Denmark and Finland backed Italy’s move and, by the weekend, 22 EU leaders had penned a letter pointing an implicit finger at Madrid over its presumed failure to “relentlessly combat illegal migration”. But what these self-ascribed doyens of border control don’t want to understand is that it’s their panic and politicking over migration that has brought us here. Ceuta is hardly a poster-child for Spain’s otherwise liberal migration policy. Rather, since the 1990s it has been the prototype for Europe’s relentless border security battle. Drones, heat detectors, motion sensors, digital watchtowers, Moroccan Auxiliary Forces: Ceuta’s border is so thoroughly militarised that it puts even Trump’s barrier-building – let alone that of Greece, Poland or Finland – to shame. The paradox, as civil guards told me when I last visited in 2023, was that this militarisation had involved ceding control. “Rabat knows it can destabilise Spain with migration,” one chief said, as he reflected on the mass entry of Moroccans in 2021 , after Madrid had angered its partner by taking in Brahim Ghali, the leader of Western Sahara’s Polisario movement, for urgent healthcare. The heavily guarded fences have become a perfect foil for staging a migration crisis. While Morocco is usually tight-lipped about its intentions, at times its ministers have bluntly said it won’t play the “ gendarme ” of Europe unless its partners support its economic and political aims. The quiet at the border since 2021 had little to do with the aggressive security hardware, and everything to do with Madrid’s 2022 endorsement of Rabat’s plan for occupied Western Sahara. So why the latest crisis? While the facts and motives are still being established, it’s unlikely to be a coincidence that, only recently, Sánchez announced a “ new phase ” in relations with Algeria – Rabat’s arch-rival and supporter of Polisario. View image in fullscreen A man attempting to escape the police, Ceuta, 2 August 2026. Photograph: Pedro Nunes/Reuters Sánchez blames the mass entry on people smugglers and misinformation about a recent Spanish supreme court ruling that prevents authorities from summarily expelling migrants who attempt to swim by sea to Spain’s territories in Africa. Yet blaming criminal organisations makes little sense: most of those who made it across were quietly returned within the day – unthinkable, if they had lost their life savings to pay smugglers. The official line from Morocco’s government is that the surge was due to “criminal organisations” and that cooperation with Spain is still “exemplary”. The social media rumour mill did mobilise people to cross; but crucially – according to Spanish intelligence – Moroccan law enforcement stopped controlling the border while its intelligence services failed to notify Spain about the online campaigns. Video clips and accounts from border crossers in numerous media outlets further suggest that law enforcement actively encouraged people to cross. It’s clear to anyone who knows the Ceuta border that nothing dramatic happens there without the Moroccan authorities letting it happen. Yet Spain is unable to call out Morocco as it desperately depends on it. Instead, both Madrid and Brussels showered Rabat with praise this past week. This is the corner the EU has painted itself into: dependent on repressive and undemocratic regimes that use migration threats for their own purposes. This has been a favoured tactic for years across the external EU borders, from Muammar Gaddafi’s threats to Ankara’s antics . And it’s all the more attractive to them thanks to the European obsession about unwanted migration – the higher the stakes, the bigger the rewards. The geopolitics are looking unfavourable to the EU. Since the Abraham accords were signed in 2020, Morocco has strengthened its hand internationally through close alliances with the Trump and Netanyahu administrations. And those two governments see Spain as their arch-foe in Europe. This January, Rabat deepened its military cooperation with Israel. In April, a US House of Representatives committee stated that Ceuta and another Spanish enclave of Melilla were “in Moroccan territory”. Israeli and Republican figures have made increasingly frequent noises of this kind. Recently, Morocco named a highway through Western Sahara after Trump. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more Preview latest after newsletter promotion Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco? Read more What all this points to is not necessarily some grand conspiracy. Rabat may well have sought to benefit opportunistically and then lost control of events. But it does suggest that what occurred in Ceuta was a geopolitical game with people as its pawns, leaving more than 70 dead . European leaders have become so obsessed with “security” that they can’t see their own best interests clearly. Notably, one of the governments waving the threat of Schengen suspension was Denmark, which should know something about geopolitical blackmail against Europe. Coercive migration pressure, evidence shows , works best when destination regions are politically divided and prone to slanging matches. This is exactly what the far right and government leaders are now indulging as they nervously blame Spain and raise the spectre of another 2015 migration crisis. Having shown their hand to “partner” states and unfriendly regimes alike, these leaders will know exactly which button to push for maximum impact. Through their reaction, EU politicians are not only undermining European solidarity – they are actively encouraging more crisis-generation, while abetting the anti-European forces in the White House and further afield. We need a different kind of migration politics that de-escalates panic instead of inviting it, that prioritises frank diplomacy over one-eyed “combat”, and that weakens the hand of hardmen and smugglers. European leaders could make a start on shifting this dynamic by not turning themselves into useful idiots at the first opportunity. Ruben Andersson is professor of social anthropology at the University of Oxford and author of Age of Security: The Rise of a Global Obsession (William Collins) out 13th August Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? According to various international media, Ratcliffe went to … Written by: Jack Williams Published on: August 25, 2026 Quick visit to Russian soil for John Ratcliffe. The CIA director flew to Moscow today, Tuesday 25 August, aboard a C-17 which departed from the Andrews base. According to various international media, Ratcliffe went to Russia for “confidential meetings”, on which no further information is known. The visit to Moscow This morning a US Air Force Boeing C-17A Globemaster III transport plane was spotted at Moscow airport together with a diplomatic motorcade. No confirmation has been received from the US and Russian governments on the identity of the US official in Russia or the purpose of the visit. The identity was revealed later by Axios journalist Barak Ravid in a post on X. 🇺🇸🇷🇺CIA director Ratcliffe visited Moscow on Tuesday. The US asked Ukraine to suspend strikes on the Russian capital until he leaves. My report on @axios https://t.co/eVVnfb8MSS — Barak Ravid (@BarakRavid) August 25, 2026 If the news is confirmed, it would be Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Russia as CIA director. U.S. intelligence has also recently played a role in recent U.S.-Russian detainee exchanges, including the April 2025 release of Ksenia Karelina, a dual U.S.-Russian citizen whose case was personally negotiated by Ratcliffe. An unusual visitor to Moscow this morning. 👀 A US Air Force C-17A Globemaster III flew from Riga to Moscow Vnukovo Airporthttps://t.co/D7vylYesDQ pic.twitter.com/jXbOSj0LXM — Flightradar24 (@flightradar24) August 25, 2026 The agency was also involved in the 2024 prisoner exchange that led to the release of Wall Street Journal journalist Evan Gershkovich and Marine veteran Paul Whelan. In November 2021, however, it was the former director of the CIA, William Burns, who went to Moscow to meet Putin and warn him against an invasion of Ukraine. The indiscretion Ratcliffe’s visit to Russia was also confirmed by an indiscretion from the Financial Times: “Last week Trump administration officials asked Kiev not to hit Moscow, St. Petersburg and the northern regions of Russia with its long-range missiles and drones on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, i.e. when the United States would send a plane carrying a high-ranking official to the Russian capital. Ukraine agreed.” The plane took off again The CIA director’s visit to Moscow lasted only a few hours: according to online global air traffic monitoring systems, the US military plane has already left for Latvia, through which it had made the outward flight during the journey from the Andrews military base, near Washington. https://www.dw.com/en/nigeria-at-least-3.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Mnvz Apart from gold, Nigeria has deposits of other valuable minerals, including tantalite, copper, and lithium Image: Stefan Heunis/AFP Advertisement At least 37 people believed to be illegal miners died Thursday while in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps (NSCDC), according to the governor of Nigeria 's north-central Niger State. "This morning we woke up to the news that about 37 persons died in the custody of the civil defense here in Minna," Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago told reporters in the state's capital. He called the incident "sad" and "tragic," adding that a committee of inquiry into the deaths had been established and was already working. The governor declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for the January elections . The police in Niger State announced that they have launched an investigation and urged relatives of the victims to come forward with any helpful information. What do we know about the incident? The suspects have been detained since the security agency made arrests on Tuesday and Wednesday due to suspicions of illegal mining in the state, said Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, head of the NSCDC in Niger, in a statement on Thursday. Aniviye said that although the agency suspects the detainees died of disease, their bodies were sent to a local hospital for a medical examination to determine the cause of death. He did not specify the type of disease. However, according to the intelligence report, "preliminary information suggests the fatalities may have resulted from overcrowding and inadequate ventilation within a detention facility." A 40-second video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men, most of whom appeared to be teenagers. Volunteers wearing gloves stood over the bodies, while veiled women tried to identify their relatives. Dirty gold: Nigeria's toxic water threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Survivors describe a lack of ventilation Dauda Shehu, one of the survivors, told the Associated Press that 65 detainees were packed into a poorly ventilated cell. "We were jampacked and there was no ventilation for us to breathe well," he said. "All of a sudden, we realized that we could not breathe and we started scrambling to get fresh air," Shehu added. The detainees tried to get the guards' attention by banging on the cell door, he explained. Spanning more than twice the area of Belgium, Niger State is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most of whom are lured by the hope of striking gold. According to officials and experts, the scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger State is also fueling violence by criminal gangs known locally as bandits. These gangs tax miners and demand a cut of the extracted ore in exchange for access to the pits. Edited by: Sean Sinico Don't let the algorithm hide the news.
